chunks: "I'd add external termination when the trace is long compared with the edge and the driver and load aren't already matched, so reflections would hurt.
The test I use is delay against rise time.
If the one-way delay of the trace is less than about a sixth of the rise time, the reflections merge into the edge and I can ignore them: that's about 28 millimetres for a one nanosecond edge.
If it's longer, I look at the mismatch. A CMOS driver of 20 ohms into a 50 ohm line and a high-impedance receiver has a source reflection of minus 0.
67 and a load reflection of plus one, so the receiver sees overshoot of tens of percent and ringing.
I'd check whether the overshoot stays inside the receiver's input range and noise margin; if it doesn't, I terminate.

Other triggers: clocks, where a false edge double-clocks something; multi-drop buses; differential and high-speed links where eye margin matters; EMI, because ringing radiates; and when the receiver has no on-die termination.

When I don't terminate: short, slow nets like GPIO, I²C and low-speed SPI where the edge is slow; interfaces where the chips have ODT built in, like DDR data; and signals where a termination would cost too much power.
It's a trade: series termination is cheap and low power, parallel termination costs DC current."
